AUS.story:
Gerald Ridsdale was ordained a Catholic priest in the Diocese of Ballarat, in Victoria, in 1961. By late 1975 his bishop, Ronald Mulkearns, knew that Ridsdale was abusing children, and kept moving him to new parishes and later to Sydney. Ridsdale was first convicted in 1993 and was eventually convicted of abusing more than 70 children.

In March 2008 the Adass Israel School, an ultra-Orthodox Jewish school in Melbourne, paid for its head teacher, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before police were told that she had abused pupils. Australia issued a warrant for 74 offences in 2014. In Israel the deputy health minister, Yaakov Litzman, pressured ministry staff to change psychiatric assessments so that she would appear unfit for extradition, the legal process of handing a suspect to another country. He later admitted breach of trust. Leifer was extradited in January 2021 and convicted in Melbourne in April 2023.

The Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse, a national public inquiry with the power to require documents, was announced in November 2012. Its final report in 2017 drew on 8,013 private sessions and evidence about 3,489 institutions; 58.1% of the survivors heard in private sessions had been abused in a religious institution and 32.5% in one run by the government. Its recommendations led to the National Redress Scheme, which began in 2018. Between 2015 and 2018 every state and territory removed or changed the limitation period, the legal deadline for suing over child abuse.

Australians also abused children abroad. In 2016 about 800 registered child sex offenders travelled overseas, often to developing countries in Asia, and 40% did not tell police. In 2020 the bank Westpac agreed to pay a A$1.3 billion penalty that included failing to check payments that could be linked to live-streamed abuse of children in the Philippines.

The Royal Commission counted abuse inside Australian institutions and led to changes in the law. Abuse paid for by Australians in other countries is known mainly through individual prosecutions and bank records.

BOL.story:
In 1964 the Spanish Jesuit priest Alfonso Pedrajas abused a child in Lima, Peru, and then settled in Bolivia, where he worked in Jesuit schools. In 1978 he confessed to a superior, who covered it up. In a diary published by the Spanish newspaper El País in 2023, Pedrajas, who died in 2009, wrote that he had abused at least 85 minors between 1972 and 2000. In May 2023 prosecutors seized internal Jesuit documents in La Paz and Cochabamba. On 2 September 2025 a Bolivian court sentenced Marcos Recolons and Ramón Alaix, former provincials, or heads of the Jesuits in Bolivia, to one year in prison each for knowing of allegations against Pedrajas and not reporting them. Sentences under three years are normally commuted in Bolivia, meaning replaced by a lighter penalty. Prosecutors said they would pursue other priests named at the trial.

Bolivia had about 150,000 Mennonites by 2023, many living in closed German-speaking farming colonies. Between 2005 and 2009, men in the Manitoba Colony sprayed a drug through bedroom windows to sedate families, then broke in and raped women and girls, including small children. The attacks were first blamed on ghosts or demons. After they came to light in June 2009, a Bolivian court in August 2011 convicted the men of raping and sexually assaulting 151 women and girls. A 2013 investigation reported similar assaults continuing.

In its 2025 report on trafficking, the US State Department said foreign offenders exploited children in rural Indigenous communities in northern La Paz department, in and around Rurrenabaque, and in tourist areas of La Paz and Beni. It said the production of abuse material for sale online was rising in Cochabamba, El Alto and Santa Cruz, and that Bolivian women and girls were exploited in sex trafficking in Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Panama and Peru.

The Jesuit superiors were convicted for failing to report, and prosecutors have said more priests may be charged. The abuse by foreign visitors and the abuse filmed for sale online are known mainly from a US government report.

CHL.story:
Paul Schäfer, a former Nazi army corporal, fled a 1959 warrant in Siegburg, Germany, for abusing two boys, and in 1961 founded Colonia Dignidad, a closed German commune in southern Chile, where he drew children from local farms into the colony's free school and clinic. In 1966 a teenager who escaped took refuge at the West German embassy, which sent a delegation and said it found no evidence. Politicians rejected escapees' allegations because of the colony's ties to those preparing the 1973 coup. Chilean officials believe the Pinochet dictatorship later used the colony to torture its opponents. An investigation opened only after Chilean mothers complained in 1997, and in 2006 a Chilean court sentenced Schäfer to 20 years for abusing 25 children.

Under the dictatorship, from 1973 to 1990, adoptions of Chilean children abroad reached their peak. Babies were taken from mainly poor mothers, some of whom were told their babies had died, and sent to families in the United States and Europe. In 2018 a judge opened a criminal investigation covering about 8,000 adoptions abroad from 1970 to 1999. In 2019 a commission of the Chamber of Deputies, the lower house of Congress, found that hospital staff, Civil Registry staff and paid private intermediaries had taken part, and that some hospitals had destroyed birth records.

In the Catholic Church, parishioners reported the Santiago priest Fernando Karadima to the archbishop in 1984, and Cardinal Errázuriz shelved a credible church investigation in 2004–05. The Vatican found Karadima guilty of sexual abuse in 2011. In 2018, after receiving a 2,300-page report by his envoy, Pope Francis wrote that he had been mistaken, and every bishop in Chile offered to resign.

In 2012 family-court judges and UNICEF interviewed children in homes supervised by SENAME, the national child protection service, and found sexual abuse was a constant; in one home in Arica, carers ran a network that sexually exploited girls.

Courts and inquiries have now examined the colony, the church hierarchy and the state's care and adoption systems. As of September 2023 nobody had been brought to justice for the adoptions abroad.

CRI.story:
Mauricio Víquez, a Catholic priest in the Archdiocese of San José who had been the church's spokesman on family issues, abused an 11-year-old boy in his parish in 2002 and 2003. The victims' lawyer later said the church had known since 2002 and did nothing. When accusations became public in 2018, Víquez left Costa Rica and travelled through Panama to San Nicolás de los Garza, in Mexico, where he was caught. The church expelled him from the clergy in 2019, and he was extradited, sent back to face trial, in 2021. In March 2022 a Costa Rican court sentenced him to 20 years for sexual abuse and rape. Three other complaints against him were declared time-barred, meaning the legal deadline for bringing them had passed. In August 2022 a civil court in San José ordered Archbishop José Rafael Quirós, the Episcopal Conference, the national body of bishops, and the church's property entity to pay 65 million colones, about US$100,000, in damages.

The US State Department's 2025 report on trafficking says traffickers exploit Costa Rican women and children for sex especially in the coastal zones of the Pacific, which tourists visit, and near the northern and southern borders, where social tolerance makes children more vulnerable. It also identifies girls from Nicaragua, Panama, the Dominican Republic and Venezuela as victims.

Víquez was convicted after he was brought back from Mexico, and three complaints against him could no longer be heard because their deadlines had passed. The sexual exploitation of children on the Pacific coast is described mainly in a US government report.

ETH.story:
Foreign adoption from Ethiopia grew from 262 children in 2002 to more than 3,887 in 2008, and 33,303 children were sent abroad between 2003 and 2022. The United States issued 15,166 visas to children adopted from Addis Ababa between 1994 and 2014, with a peak of 2,514 in 2010. Orphanages and foreign agencies arranged the adoptions. Canadian families reported orphan papers for children whose parents were alive, and the US State Department found the agency Better Futures Adoption Services involved in child trafficking; it lost its licence in 2011. Ireland suspended adoptions from Ethiopia in 2007, Australia in 2009 and Denmark in 2016. Ethiopia suspended foreign adoptions in November 2017, and in January 2018 its parliament banned adoption by foreigners, citing abuse and neglect of children abroad. In Belgium, a Flemish review of Ethiopian adoptions from 1997 to 2015 found that in the worst cases birth parents had not given up their children voluntarily.

During the war that began in 2020, all sides sexually abused girls. The International Commission of Human Rights Experts on Ethiopia, a UN-appointed investigative panel, reported in 2022 widespread sexual violence by Ethiopian and Eritrean forces in Tigray, and rapes by Tigrayan forces of girls as young as 11 in Amhara villages in 2021. In February 2021 the BBC reported that 200 girls under 18 had registered as rape survivors at health facilities in Mekelle. The UN verified sexual violence against 73 children in 2024, 38 of them by the Ethiopian National Defence Forces, the national army.

The US State Department's 2025 trafficking report says Ethiopian girls are exploited in domestic servitude and sex trafficking in Djibouti and Sudan, and children in organised begging rings in Saudi Arabia. It says reports of official complicity continued.

Ethiopia ended foreign adoption in 2018, and receiving countries such as Belgium are still examining how earlier adoptions were arranged. In 2024 the UN was still verifying sexual violence against children by the national army.

GNQ.story:
Between December 2013 and June 2014, boys aged about 8 to 13 sheltering at the M'Poko camp in Bangui, the capital of the Central African Republic, said soldiers had sexually abused them, often in exchange for food or money. Most of the soldiers they named belonged to the French Sangaris force. Others were Chadian and Equatorial Guinean troops serving in the MISCA force.

In December 2015 a panel appointed by the UN Secretary-General and chaired by Marie Deschamps reported that the UN's handling of the boys' accounts had been a "gross institutional failure". The report had passed "from inbox to inbox", and the panel found that three senior UN officials had abused their authority. Soldiers on such missions can be tried only by their own country, and the UN can only send them home. The records for this map include no trial in Equatorial Guinea.

Inside Equatorial Guinea, the abuse of children has barely been measured. In its 2026 update, Childlight, a research centre that combines representative surveys into global estimates, found no such survey data on the online sexual exploitation of children for West and Central Africa.

The one documented case concerns Equatorial Guinean soldiers abroad. Without surveys or inquiries, how many children are abused inside the country is unknown.

IND.story:
In 2018 the Bihar state government asked Koshish, a unit of the Tata Institute of Social Sciences, to audit 110 children's homes funded by its social welfare department. The audit, submitted in April 2018, graded a girls' home in Muzaffarpur, run by the organisation of Brajesh Thakur, a politically connected man, as criminal negligence, and raised abuse at 14 other homes. Police registered a case on 31 May 2018, and medical examinations indicated that 34 girls, most of them children, had been sexually abused. Bihar's social welfare minister, Manju Verma, resigned. Because the accused were influential in Bihar, the Supreme Court moved the trial to Delhi, where in January 2020 a court convicted Thakur and 18 others. In Deoria, in Uttar Pradesh, police rescued 24 girls from a shelter in 2018; the state minister said the charity's recognition and funds had been withdrawn a year earlier, and the home had kept operating.

Political status also delayed a case against a legislator. In Unnao, a member of the Uttar Pradesh legislature, Kuldeep Singh Sengar, raped a girl in 2017. Her father died in police custody, and Sengar was arrested only after the Allahabad High Court ordered it in 2018. He was convicted in 2019 and sentenced to life.

India also sent 12,511 children abroad for adoption between 2003 and 2022. In 2001 police in Andhra Pradesh exposed a home that had earned Rs 3.33 crore from foreign adoptions, mainly to the United States; in 2005 ten people were sentenced, and the state barred private agencies from placing children.

The US State Department's 2025 report says traffickers bring significant numbers of Nepali and Bangladeshi women and girls into India for sex. In Kolkata in 2015, six young women freed from brothels all carried false adult identity papers, which the charity International Justice Mission said traffickers issue to underage girls.

India has held no national inquiry into abuse in institutions, and Childlight found no representative survey data on online exploitation for South Asia. Its convictions have come from state audits and single cases, and the national scale is unknown.

JAM.story:
In December 2002, after a public campaign about abuse in children's homes, the Government of Jamaica appointed a four-member panel chaired by Sadie Keating to review the care of children in state custody. Its report in 2003 found that children in children's homes and places of safety had been sexually abused, including by the staff employed to care for them. Nine of the 15 homes the panel visited could not recall an inspection by the Child Services Division, the government office responsible for them, in the previous three years.

The US State Department's 2025 report on trafficking cites a 2023 study that estimated 6.3 percent of Jamaican children aged 12 to 17 had experienced conditions indicating trafficking. It says children are exploited for sex in resort areas visited by tourists, sometimes with their parents' involvement, and that in some communities men pay girls or their families for sex. Those involved include family members, local strongmen known as "dons", and foreign and local buyers. The report says corruption and official complicity, including within law enforcement, remained significant concerns.

The official record on Jamaica consists of one review of state care in 2003 and a foreign government report in 2025, so little is known about what changed in between.

LKA.story:
In the 1980s babies in Sri Lanka were bought or taken from hospitals, handed to women paid to pose as their mothers in court, and sold for adoption abroad. About 4,000 went to the Netherlands, and others to the UK, Sweden, Denmark and Germany. Brokers, doctors and nurses acted as intermediaries for Western adoption agencies, and adoption records were widely falsified. In 1987 a police raid on a "baby farm" found 20 newborns and 22 women, and Sri Lanka imposed a temporary ban on foreign adoptions. In 2017, after a Dutch television documentary, the health minister, Rajitha Senaratne, acknowledged that "there were a lot of baby farms back then" and announced an inquiry and a DNA databank.

Between 2004 and 2007 Sri Lankan soldiers serving with the UN mission in Haiti exploited children there. An Associated Press investigation in 2017 found that at least 134 of them had exploited at least nine children in a sex ring. The UN's internal investigators found the abuse was frequent and happened at almost every place the contingent was deployed. UN peacekeepers can be prosecuted only by their own country. In 2007, 108 soldiers, including three officers, were sent home; Sri Lankan authorities judged the acts "consensual", nobody was jailed, and in 2016 one victim received a one-off ex gratia payment, a payment made without admitting legal liability.

In Sri Lanka, complaints about a Buddhist monk who ran a home for war-affected Tamil children in Vavuniya reached the National Child Protection Authority, the government's child protection agency, from 2010. He was arrested in October 2013, after protests by local child protection officers, for abusing a 9-year-old. In December he received unconditional bail after the Attorney General's Department, on the Authority's instructions, told the court it had no objection.

Sri Lanka's government admitted the baby farms in 2017, and the fullest findings on how the adoptions were arranged come from inquiries in the Netherlands and Switzerland. No Sri Lankan soldier has been jailed for the abuse in Haiti.

NLD.story:
In March 2010 the Catholic Church in the Netherlands set up a commission led by the former minister Wim Deetman to investigate abuse by its clergy. Its report in December 2011 identified at least 800 priests, monks and other members of religious orders who had abused children between 1945 and 1985, 105 of them still alive, and estimated that 10,000 to 20,000 minors had been abused. It found that bishops and church officials had known and followed a policy of "not hanging out the dirty washing", that is, of avoiding scandal.

Inquiries into the state's own care system followed. In 2012 a commission chaired by Rieke Samson, a former senior prosecutor, received 800 claims of sexual abuse of children placed in care since 1945, 65% about children's homes and 30% about foster families, and passed 42 files to the public prosecutor. In 2019 a commission led by Micha de Winter found that a considerable share of children in youth care since 1945 had not been protected from physical, psychological and sexual violence, and that the government had done too little.

The Netherlands also received children from abroad for adoption, including 4,099 from South Korea between 1969 and 2003 and about 4,000 from Sri Lanka in the 1980s. In February 2021 a government committee chaired by Tjibbe Joustra found serious violations in adoptions from 1967 to 1997/98 and concluded that the Dutch government had for decades failed to prevent them. The government suspended all intercountry adoption that month, and in May 2024 announced that citizens would no longer be allowed to adopt from abroad.

Dutch servers have hosted much of the world's abuse material. In 2018, 47% of the material acted on by the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds such images, was hosted in the Netherlands. In 2025 the share was 11%, or 33,788 internet addresses.

The church, state care and foreign adoption have each been examined by an inquiry, and adoption from abroad is being ended. The country's National Rapporteur reported exploitation cases rising from 868 in 2023 to 944 in 2024, with more teenage victims.

PAN.story:
In early February 2021 a subcommission of Panama's National Assembly, the national parliament, reported abuse in shelters for children at social risk. The shelters were run by private organisations and charities under the supervision of Senniaf, the government's secretariat for children, adolescents and the family. By March 2021 the Public Ministry, Panama's prosecution service, had opened 18 criminal investigations, inspected 57 shelters and interviewed about 280 children. It identified 20 victims, who were moved, and charged five people with offences including mistreating children, embezzlement and sexual offences. The Ombudsman, an official who investigates complaints against the state, found irregularities in 34% of 52 shelters inspected and found that 70% of 44 shelters lacked suitable staff and that Senniaf did little follow-up.

In 2023 an independent commission appointed by SOS Children's Villages, an international charity that runs children's homes, named Panama among the countries in its report, which confirmed serious allegations of sexual and physical abuse of children in several of the charity's national associations in Africa, Asia and Central America.

In October 2024, after an alert from Spanish police investigating a network sharing abuse material, Panama's police arrested a man in La Chorrera accused of contacting children through the gaming platform Roblox and threatening them to obtain sexual images. Panama also hosts some of this material. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds and removes abuse images, took action against 5,275 internet addresses there, 2% of its total.

The 2021 findings led to charges against five people and showed that the agency responsible for the shelters had done little to check on them. No later official review of the shelters is recorded.

SSD.story:
The Lord's Resistance Army, a rebel group from northern Uganda, abducted tens of thousands of children to use as fighters, porters and "wives". From 1994 to 2006 it held abducted Ugandan children at bases in southern Sudan, and from 2008 it abducted thousands more in South Sudan, DR Congo and the Central African Republic. In 2021 the International Criminal Court convicted one of its commanders, Dominic Ongwen, of 61 crimes including rape, sexual slavery and forced marriage. A warrant for its leader, Joseph Kony, is outstanding.

In March 2022 the UN Commission on Human Rights in South Sudan, a panel of investigators reporting to the UN Human Rights Council, found that the parties to the country's conflict used rape of women and girls to terrorise and repress people. It found that abductions of women and girls for forced marriage and sexual slavery had increased in Jonglei, the Greater Pibor Administrative Area, Warrap and Lakes. A military court in Yei had convicted soldiers of the national army, the South Sudan People's Defence Forces (SSPDF), of rape in late 2020, but the victims had not been paid the compensation the court ordered. The UN verified sexual violence against 94 girls, some as young as 7, in 2022, 74 of them by the SSPDF, and against 7 girls in 2024, 5 by the SSPDF.

People who fled to camps were also exploited. In 2022 The New Humanitarian and Al Jazeera reported that between 2015 and 2022 aid workers in the UN-run camp for displaced people at Malakal exploited women and girls, including by trading aid for sex; staff of IOM, MSF, WFP and World Vision were among those named. Peacekeepers accused of abuse can be prosecuted only by their own country, and the UN can only send them home. Few such cases are finalised; in one, a Togolese officer was sent home and imprisoned for 60 days.

Most of what is known about children in South Sudan comes from UN verification and journalists. In 2025 the US CyberTipline, the main international channel for reports of online abuse, received 863 reports for the country.

TLS.story:
Indonesia occupied Timor-Leste until 1999. In 2005 the Commission for Reception, Truth and Reconciliation (CAVR) published its final report, Chega!, which found that at least 4,000 children had been taken from their families and moved illegally to Indonesia during the occupation. Indonesian military units took some of them and used them as child soldiers or servants, and Islamic organisations took others and converted them. The children were often renamed and lost contact with their families. CAVR and a joint Indonesia–Timor-Leste truth commission recommended a commission to search for the missing children, and none was created.

In 1992 Richard Daschbach, a US-born missionary priest of the Society of the Divine Word, a Catholic order, founded the Topu Honis children's shelter in Oecusse. After a complaint in February 2018 he admitted abusing children to his superiors, and the Vatican dismissed him from the priesthood that November without telling the public. He was arrested in April 2019. A report by the Dili archdiocese's Justice and Peace Commission defended him. In December 2021 a court in Oecusse sentenced him to 12 years, on the testimony of four victims.

In 2019 the Vatican received allegations that Bishop Carlos Ximenes Belo, a Salesian priest and Nobel Peace laureate, had abused boys in Fatumaca and Dili. In 2020 it limited his movements and ministry and barred him from contact with minors and with Timor-Leste. It disclosed these sanctions only in September 2022, the day after the Dutch magazine De Groene Amsterdammer reported that two men said Belo had abused them.

No commission has searched for the children taken to Indonesia. In both church cases the Vatican imposed penalties without telling the public.

YEM.story:
In September 2019 the Group of Eminent Experts on Yemen, a panel mandated by the UN Human Rights Council, reported that the Security Belt Forces had raped 18 women, four boys and a girl between 2016 and 2019, and had committed widespread rape of migrant women, girls and boys at a former facility in Aden. It also found that members of the Yemeni army's 35th Armoured Brigade raped two boys, that personnel from the United Arab Emirates at Al-Bureiqa raped a boy, and that a 17-year-old boy suffered sexual violence in a detention site run by the Houthis, the armed movement that acts as the government where it rules. In 2020 the Group found credible accounts that the Houthis had recruited 34 girls aged 13 to 17 between June 2015 and June 2020, 12 of whom reportedly suffered sexual violence, forced early marriage linked to their recruitment, or both. The Group said its figures were a small sample.

The UN's own verification continued after the Group's reports. It verified sexual violence against 24 children in 2023, 8 boys and 16 girls, 20 of them by the Yemen Armed Forces and allied forces, including the police. In 2024 it verified 11 cases, attributed to the Houthis, the Yemen Armed Forces and allied forces.

Childlight, a research centre that combines representative surveys into global estimates, found no such survey data on the online sexual exploitation of children for the Middle East and North Africa in its 2026 update.

Government forces, their allies and the Houthis were all still named in the UN's 2024 count. Because there are no surveys and the experts called their figures a small sample, the number of children affected is unknown.
